claim: Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques have the potential to improve memory functions.
source: Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques have the potential to improve memory functions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the study's premise, supported by the broader literature context provided in the introduction.

claim: The results of non-invasive brain stimulation on memory have been relatively modest and time-consuming.
source: However, the results so far have been relatively modest and time-consuming.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction discussing the limited effects of NIBS techniques.

claim: A novel 3-min combination of personalized repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (intermittent theta burst, iTBS) coupled with simultaneous application of gamma transcranial alternating current stimulation (γtACS) over the precuneus was implemented to modulate long-term memory in healthy subjects.
source: Here, we implemented a novel 3-min combination of personalized repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (intermittent theta burst, iTBS) coupled with simultaneous application of gamma transcranial alternating current stimulation (γtACS) over the precuneus, a brain area connected with the hippocampus, to modulate long-term memory in healthy subjects.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol implemented in the study.

claim: The precuneus is a brain area connected with the hippocampus.
source: over the precuneus, a brain area connected with the hippocampus
evidence: This is supported by anatomical knowledge and citations in the introduction about precuneus connectivity.

claim: Only dual electromagnetic stimulation of the precuneus produced an increase in long-term associative memory as compared to iTBS alone and sham conditions in a sample of healthy volunteers.
source: Only dual electromagnetic stimulation of the precuneus produced an increase in long-term associative memory as compared to iTBS alone and sham conditions in a sample of healthy volunteers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from experiment 1.

claim: The effects of dual stimulation on associative memory were replicated in another independent sample.
source: The effects were replicated in another independent sample, in which the increased associative memory was retained for up to 1 week.
evidence: This is supported by data from experiment 2.

claim: The increased associative memory from dual stimulation was retained for up to 1 week.
source: The effects were replicated in another independent sample, in which the increased associative memory was retained for up to 1 week.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal data from experiment 2.

claim: Dual stimulation increased gamma oscillations.
source: Moreover, dual stimulation increased gamma oscillations and precuneus–hippocampus functional connectivity through the white matter tracts linking the precuneus with the temporal lobe.
evidence: This is supported by TMS-EEG data from experiment 3.

claim: Dual stimulation increased precuneus–hippocampus functional connectivity through the white matter tracts linking the precuneus with the temporal lobe.
source: Moreover, dual stimulation increased gamma oscillations and precuneus–hippocampus functional connectivity through the white matter tracts linking the precuneus with the temporal lobe.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI and DTI data from experiment 4.

claim: Dual stimulation may lead neuronal assemblies in a state favorable to enhance long-term plasticity.
source: These findings show that dual stimulation may lead neuronal assemblies in a state favorable to enhance long-term plasticity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed increases in gamma oscillations and connectivity.

claim: Personalized dual electromagnetic stimulation of the precuneus may represent a new powerful approach for enhancing memory functions in several healthy and clinical conditions.
source: Personalized dual electromagnetic stimulation of the precuneus may represent a new powerful approach for enhancing memory functions in several healthy and clinical conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The prevalence of age-related memory deficits is growing as the world's population ages.
source: As the world's population ages, the prevalence of age-related memory deficits is growing.
evidence: This is based on general demographic knowledge.

claim: Age-related memory deficits often signal the onset of more severe cognitive decline.
source: This phenomenon often signals the onset of more severe cognitive decline, which has a strong impact on society.
evidence: This is based on clinical knowledge about cognitive decline progression.

claim: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques have been largely used to enhance human cognition in the last two decades.
source: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques have been largely used to enhance human cognition in the last two decades (Antal et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Encouraging results with NIBS have been reported in both healthy and pathological conditions, including depression, stroke, and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Encouraging results have been reported in both healthy and pathological conditions, including depression, stroke, and Alzheimer's disease (Blumberger et al., 2018; Koch et al., 2022; Lefaucheur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) are two forms of NIBS widely used to enhance memory performance.
source: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) are two forms of NIBS widely used to enhance memory performance (Grover et al., 2022; Koch et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using these techniques for memory enhancement.

claim: rTMS induces depolarization of cortical neuronal assemblies and leads to after-effects that have been linked to changes in synaptic plasticity involving mechanisms of long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: rTMS, based on the principle of Faraday, induces depolarization of cortical neuronal assemblies and leads to after-effects that have been linked to changes in synaptic plasticity involving mechanisms of long-term potentiation (LTP) (Huang et al., 2017; Jannati et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the mechanisms of rTMS.

claim: tACS causes rhythmic fluctuations in neuronal membrane potentials, which can bias spike timing, leading to an entrainment of the neural activity.
source: On the other hand, tACS causes rhythmic fluctuations in neuronal membrane potentials, which can bias spike timing, leading to an entrainment of the neural activity (Wischnewski et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing the mechanisms of tACS.

claim: The induction of gamma oscillatory activity has been proposed to play an important role in spike timing-dependent plasticity.
source: In particular, the induction of gamma oscillatory activity has been proposed to play an important role in a type of LTP known as spike timing-dependent plasticity, which depends on a precise temporal delay between the firing of a presynaptic and a postsynaptic neuron (Griffiths and Jensen, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a theoretical framework.

claim: Both LTP and gamma oscillations have a strong link with memory processes such as encoding.
source: Both LTP and gamma oscillations have a strong link with memory processes such as encoding (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Griffiths and Jensen, 2023; Rossi et al., 2001), pointing to rTMS and tACS as good candidates for memory enhancement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies on LTP and memory.

claim: The overall effects of rTMS and tACS on memory are relatively modest, even with prolonged stimulation sessions.
source: However, despite the increasing expectations, their overall effects are relatively modest, even with prolonged stimulation sessions (Grover et al., 2022; Polanía et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to meta-analyses and reviews.

claim: The behavioral and clinical effects of NIBS are extremely variable.
source: In fact, the behavioral and clinical effects are extremely variable (Corp et al., 2020), especially when used to modulate memory functions (Pabst et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting variability in NIBS effects.

claim: The simultaneous application of tACS in the range of the gamma frequency band (γtACS) with intermittent theta burst (iTBS) enhances the after-effects of iTBS alone on the motor and prefrontal cortices.
source: Recent studies explored the possibility of combining these two techniques, showing that the simultaneous application of tACS in the range of the gamma frequency band (γtACS) with intermittent theta burst (iTBS), an rTMS protocol known to induce LTP (Huang et al., 2005), enhances the after-effects of iTBS alone on the motor and prefrontal cortices (Guerra et al., 2018; Maiella et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: iTBS is an rTMS protocol known to induce LTP.
source: intermittent theta burst (iTBS), an rTMS protocol known to induce LTP (Huang et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original iTBS protocol paper.

claim: Long-term memory formation has been associated with the neural activity of the precuneus (PC).
source: Long-term memory formation has been associated with the neural activity of the precuneus (PC).
evidence: This is supported by citations in the following sentences.

claim: The PC represents one of the main hubs of the default mode network.
source: The PC represents one of the main hubs of the default mode network (Cavanna and Trimble, 2006; Cunningham et al., 2017; Jitsuishi and Yamaguchi, 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroanatomical studies.

claim: The PC is involved in the formation of associative, episodic, and autobiographic memories.
source: and is involved in the formation of associative, episodic, and autobiographic memories (Bonnì et al., 2015; Brodt et al., 2018; Flanagin et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to memory studies.

claim: The PC is connected with the temporal lobe and the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, it is connected with the temporal lobe and the hippocampus (Cunningham et al., 2017; Dadario and Sughrue, 2023; Tanglay et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to connectivity studies.

claim: The PC represents an ideal target for NIBS to modulate memory functions with profound clinical implications, such as in the case of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Hence, the PC represents an ideal target for NIBS to modulate memory functions with profound clinical implications, such as in the case of Alzheimer's disease (Koch et al., 2025; Koch et al., 2024; Koch et al., 2022; Koch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies by the authors.

claim: γtACS would activate key neural mechanisms underlying memory formation, favoring the iTBS-mediated plasticity induction by entraining and synchronizing endogenous gamma oscillations.
source: Here, we hypothesized that γtACS would activate key neural mechanisms underlying memory formation, favoring the iTBS-mediated plasticity induction by entraining and synchronizing endogenous gamma oscillations, thereby improving long-term memory.
evidence: This is the study's hypothesis, based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: The dual application of iTBS and γtACS over the PC could be a promising tool for memory enhancement by enhancing plasticity mechanisms.
source: Thus, we reasoned that the dual application of iTBS and γtACS over the PC could be a promising tool for memory enhancement by enhancing plasticity mechanisms.
evidence: This is the study's rationale, based on the hypothesis.

claim: In experiment 1, subjects (n = 20) were asked to perform two tasks measuring long- and short-term memory performances immediately after three balanced, randomized, and double-blind stimulation conditions with a cross-over design.
source: In the first experiment, subjects (n = 20) were asked to perform two tasks measuring long- and short-term memory performances immediately after three balanced, randomized, and double-blind stimulation conditions with a cross-over design (iTBS + γtACS, iTBS + sham-tACS, sham-iTBS + sham-tACS).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of experiment 1.

claim: Stimulation parameters were personalized and identified using functional MRI (fMRI) and TMS–EEG.
source: Stimulation parameters were personalized and identified using functional MRI (fMRI) and TMS–EEG (see Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This describes the personalization approach, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Long-term memory was assessed by the face–name associative task (FNAT), requiring the memorization of 12 faces with corresponding names and occupations.
source: Long-term memory was assessed by the face–name associative task (FNAT), requiring the memorization of 12 faces with corresponding names and occupations
evidence: This describes the FNAT task used in the study.

claim: Short-term memory was assessed by the short-term memory binding test (STMB).
source: while short-term memory was assessed by the short-term memory binding test (STMB) (see Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the STMB task used in the study.

claim: The different stimulation protocols were all well-tolerated.
source: The different stimulation protocols were all well-tolerated.
evidence: This is a safety observation from the study.

claim: No one reported significant side effects connected with the neuromodulation protocol applications.
source: No one reported significant side effects connected with the neuromodulation protocol applications.
evidence: This is a safety observation from the study.

claim: Dual iTBS + γtACS improved long-term associative memory as compared to the other conditions.
source: We found that dual iTBS + γtACS improved long-term associative memory as compared to the other conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiment 1.

claim: Dual iTBS + γtACS increased the performance in recalling the association between face, name, and occupation (FNAT accuracy), both for the immediate (F2,38 = 7.18; p = 0.002; η²p = 0.274) and the delayed (F2,38 = 5.86; p = 0.006; η²p = 0.236) recall performances.
source: Dual iTBS + γtACS increased the performance in recalling the association between face, name, and occupation (FNAT accuracy), both for the immediate (F2,38 = 7.18; p = 0.002; η²p = 0.274) and the delayed (F2,38 = 5.86; p = 0.006; η²p = 0.236) recall performances (Figure 2, panel A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of FNAT data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The sensitivity analysis showed a minimal detectable effect size of η²p = 0.215 with 20 participants.
source: The sensitivity analysis showed a minimal detectable effect size of η²p = 0.215 with 20 participants.
evidence: This is a statistical power calculation for experiment 1.

claim: Post hoc analysis showed an advantage for dual iTBS + γtACS as compared to iTBS + sham-tACS condition for the immediate recall (40.0 ± 21.6% vs. 25.0 ± 17.9%, p = 0.002 Bonferroni corrected, corresponding to a relative improvement of 63.79%).
source: Post hoc analysis showed an advantage for dual iTBS + γtACS as compared to iTBS + sham-tACS condition for the immediate (40.0 ± 21.6% vs. 25.0 ± 17.9%, p = 0.002 Bonferroni corrected, corresponding to a relative improvement of 63.79%)
evidence: This is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of FNAT immediate recall data.

claim: Post hoc analysis showed an advantage for dual iTBS + γtACS as compared to iTBS + sham-tACS condition for the delayed recall (34.2 ± 20.4% vs. 24.2 ± 19.8%, p < 0.05 Bonferroni corrected, corresponding to a relative improvement of 34.16%).
source: and for the delayed recall (34.2 ± 20.4% vs. 24.2 ± 19.8%, p < 0.05 Bonferroni corrected, corresponding to a relative improvement of 34.16%)
evidence: This is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of FNAT delayed recall data.

claim: Post hoc analysis showed an advantage for dual iTBS + γtACS as compared to the sham-iTBS + sham-tACS condition for the delayed recall (34.2 ± 20.4% vs. 26.3 ± 17.6%, p=0.037 Bonferroni corrected, corresponding to a relative improvement of 34.04%).
source: as well as compared to the sham-iTBS + sham-tACS condition for the delayed recall (34.2 ± 20.4% vs. 26.3 ± 17.6%, p=0.037 Bonferroni corrected, corresponding to a relative improvement of 34.04%) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of FNAT delayed recall data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Dual iTBS + γtACS increased the performance in the association between face and name (FNAT NAME) delayed recall (F2,38 = 3.46; p = 0.042; η²p = 0.154; iTBS + γtACS vs. sham-iTBS + sham-tACS: 42.9 ± 21.5% vs. 33.8 ± 19%; p = 0.048 Bonferroni corrected).
source: The in-depth analysis of the FNAT accuracy investigating the specific contribution of face–name and face–occupation recall revealed that dual iTBS + γtACS increased the performance in the association between face and name (FNAT NAME) delayed recall (F2,38 = 3.46; p = 0.042; η²p = 0.154; iTBS + γtACS vs. sham-iTBS + sham-tACS: 42.9 ± 21.5% vs. 33.8 ± 19%; p = 0.048 Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in-depth analysis of FNAT data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: iTBS + sham-tACS did not result in any improvement as compared to sham-iTBS + sham-tACS.
source: iTBS + sham-tACS did not result in any improvement as compared to sham-iTBS + sham-tACS.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: No significant effects were found over the recall of the association between face and occupation (FNAT OCCUPATION) (p < 0.05).
source: No significant effects were found over the recall of the association between face and occupation (FNAT OCCUPATION) (p < 0.05).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The effects of dual iTBS + γtACS stimulation were selective for long-term but not short-term memory, since no effects were found on STMB accuracy and RTs (all ps >0.05).
source: Moreover, we found that the effects of dual iTBS + γtACS stimulation were selective for long-term but not short-term memory, since no effects were found on STMB accuracy and RTs (all ps >0.05) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the absence of significant effects on STMB shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Biophysical modeling calculations showed that the iTBS induced a mean e-field of 29.55 ± 5.17 V/m.
source: Biophysical modeling calculations showed that the iTBS induced a mean e-field of 29.55 ± 5.17 V/m
evidence: This is based on computational modeling of the electric field.

claim: γtACS led to a much smaller mean e-field of 0.1 ± 0.55 V/m.
source: while γtACS led to a much smaller mean e-field of 0.1 ± 0.55 V/m.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling of the electric field.

claim: In experiment 2, an independent sample (n = 10) was used to confirm the effects of dual iTBS + γtACS and to investigate the time course of memory retention.
source: To confirm the above-described effects of dual iTBS + γtACS on an independent sample (n = 10) and to investigate the time course of memory retention, we performed a second experiment.
evidence: This describes the purpose and design of experiment 2.

claim: In experiment 2, subjects were asked to execute the delayed FNAT cued recall 24 hr and 1 week after the neuromodulatory protocols.
source: In this experiment, subjects were asked to execute the delayed FNAT cued recall 24 hr and 1 week after the neuromodulatory protocols.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of experiment 2.

claim: Experiment 2 confirmed that dual iTBS + γtACS improved immediate recall at TOTAL FNAT as compared to iTBS + sham-tACS (F1,9 = 7.31; p = 0.024; η²p = 0.448; 26.7 ± 10.2% vs. 17.5 ± 8.3%; p = 0.024 corresponding to a relative improvement of 82.50%).
source: As for experiment 1, we confirmed that dual iTBS + γtACS improved immediate recall at TOTAL FNAT as compared to iTBS + sham-tACS (F1,9 = 7.31; p = 0.024; η²p = 0.448; 26.7 ± 10.2% vs. 17.5 ± 8.3%; p = 0.024 corresponding to a relative improvement of 82.50%) (see Supplementary file 2 for statistical details).
evidence: This is a replication finding from experiment 2.

claim: The sensitivity analysis for experiment 2 showed a minimal detectable effect size of η²p = 0.388 with 10 participants.
source: The sensitivity analysis showed a minimal detectable effect size of η²p = 0.388 with 10 participants.
evidence: This is a statistical power calculation for experiment 2.

claim: Dual iTBS + γtACS exerted a long-lasting effect on long-term associative memory (F1,9 = 8.433; p = 0.017; η²p=0.484).
source: More importantly, we found that dual iTBS + γtACS exerted a long-lasting effect on long-term associative memory (F1,9 = 8.433; p = 0.017; η²p=0.484) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal data from experiment 2 shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The incremental effect on TOTAL FNAT performance was still evident at 24 hr after the neuromodulation (day 2: 25 ± 9.6% vs. 14.2 ± 9.7%, t9 = −2.89, p = 0.009 corresponding to a relative improvement of 88.33%).
source: We observed that the incremental effect on TOTAL FNAT performance was still evident at 24 hr and 1 week after the neuromodulation (day 1: 25.8 ± 10.7% vs. 15 ± 9.5%, t9 = −2.75, p = 0.011 corresponding to a relative improvement of 78.33%; day 2: 25 ± 9.6% vs. 14.2 ± 9.7%, t9 = −2.89, p = 0.009 corresponding to a relative improvement of 88.33%; day 7: 23.3 ± 12.9% vs. 14.2 ± 12.5%, t9 = −2.40, p = 0.020 corresponding to a relative improvement of 80%) (see Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal data from experiment 2.

claim: The incremental effect on TOTAL FNAT performance was still evident at 1 week after the neuromodulation (day 7: 23.3 ± 12.9% vs. 14.2 ± 12.5%, t9 = −2.40, p = 0.020 corresponding to a relative improvement of 80%).
source: We observed that the incremental effect on TOTAL FNAT performance was still evident at 24 hr and 1 week after the neuromodulation (day 1: 25.8 ± 10.7% vs. 15 ± 9.5%, t9 = −2.75, p = 0.011 corresponding to a relative improvement of 78.33%; day 2: 25 ± 9.6% vs. 14.2 ± 9.7%, t9 = −2.89, p = 0.009 corresponding to a relative improvement of 88.33%; day 7: 23.3 ± 12.9% vs. 14.2 ± 12.5%, t9 = −2.40, p = 0.020 corresponding to a relative improvement of 80%) (see Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal data from experiment 2.

claim: No significant effects were found for STMB accuracy and RTs (all ps > 0.05) in experiment 2.
source: No significant effects were found for STMB accuracy and RTs (all ps > 0.05) as for experiment 1 (see the Supplementary file 2 for statistical details).
evidence: This is a negative finding from experiment 2.

claim: Experiment 3 investigated the effects of the neuromodulation protocol on cortical oscillations (TMS-related spectral perturbation, TRSP) and excitability (TMS-evoked potentials, TEPs), through TMS–EEG recordings (n = 14 subjects, 6 of those also participated in experiment 1).
source: We then aimed to investigate the effects of the neuromodulation protocol on cortical oscillations (TMS-related spectral perturbation, TRSP) and excitability (TMS-evoked potentials, TEPs), through TMS–EEG recordings (n = 14 subjects, 6 of those also participated in experiment 1).
evidence: This describes the purpose and design of experiment 3.

claim: Cortical oscillations in the gamma band increased after dual iTBS + γtACS as compared to baseline TMS–EEG recordings (stimulation F1,13 = 5.073; p = 0.042; η²p = 0.281).
source: We found that cortical oscillations in the gamma band increased after dual iTBS + γtACS as compared to baseline TMS–EEG recordings (stimulation F1,13 = 5.073; p = 0.042; η²p = 0.281) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by TMS-EEG data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An increase in the gamma-TRSP was observed after dual iTBS + γtACS as compared to iTBS +sham-tACS in both time points (ΔT1: 0.045 ± 0.09 to −0.013 ± 0.06; t13 = 1.96; p = 0.036; ΔT2: 0.026 ± 0.04 to −0.013 ± 0.05; t13 = 1.92; p = 0.039).
source: Specifically, we observed an increase in the gamma-TRSP after dual iTBS + γtACS as compared to iTBS +sham-tACS in both time points (ΔT1: 0.045 ± 0.09 to −0.013 ± 0.06; t13 = 1.96; p = 0.036; ΔT2: 0.026 ± 0.04 to −0.013 ± 0.05; t13 = 1.92; p = 0.039) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by TMS-EEG data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of increased gamma oscillations was specific to PC; no significant effect was found when testing TMS–EEG over the left posterior parietal cortex (l-PPC) (p > 0.05).
source: This effect was specific to PC; indeed, no significant effect was found when testing TMS–EEG over the left posterior parietal cortex (l-PPC) (p > 0.05).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing spatial specificity.

claim: Increased cortical excitability was evident after dual iTBS + γtACS but not after iTBS + sham-tACS condition.
source: This result was reflected by increased cortical excitability evident after dual iTBS + γtACS but not after iTBS + sham-tACS condition (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by TEP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A significant TEP amplitude increase was observed over a cluster of parietal and occipital electrodes comparing T0 vs. T1 (mean t-value13 = −3.29; all ps < 0.05).
source: Specifically, we observed a significant TEP amplitude increase over a cluster of parietal and occipital electrodes comparing T0 vs. T1 (mean t-value13 = −3.29; all ps < 0.05)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of TEP data.

claim: A significant TEP amplitude increase was observed over POz (t-value13 = −4.74; p < 0.05) when comparing T0 vs. T2.
source: and over POz (t-value13 = −4.74; p < 0.05) when comparing T0 vs. T2.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of TEP data.

claim: No significant differences in TEP were found comparing T0 vs. T1 and T2 in the iTBS + sham-tACS condition (ps > 0.05).
source: No significant differences were found comparing T0 vs. T1 and T2 in the iTBS + sham-tACS condition (ps > 0.05).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the control condition.

claim: Experiment 4 investigated the effects of the dual iTBS + γtACS protocols on MRI-based resting state functional connectivity (n = 16 subjects, 7 of whom participated in experiment 1).
source: Finally, we investigated the effects of the dual iTBS + γtACS protocols on MRI-based resting state functional connectivity (n = 16 subjects, 7 of whom participated in experiment 1).
evidence: This describes the purpose and design of experiment 4.

claim: ROI-to-ROI analysis revealed a significant difference specifically for the connectivity between the PC and the hippocampi (F3,13 = 5.78, p-FDR = 0.029).
source: Region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI analysis revealed a significant difference specifically for the connectivity between the PC and the hippocampi (F3,13 = 5.78, p-FDR = 0.029).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI connectivity analysis.

claim: Post hoc analysis showed increased connectivity between PC and hippocampi after the stimulation for the dual iTBS + γtACS (t15 = 3.67, p-FDR = 0.0023).
source: Post hoc analysis showed increased connectivity after the stimulation for the dual iTBS + γtACS (t15 = 3.67, p-FDR = 0.0023; Figure 4A), but not for the iTBS + sham-tACS.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI connectivity analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No increased connectivity between PC and hippocampi was found for the iTBS + sham-tACS condition.
source: Post hoc analysis showed increased connectivity after the stimulation for the dual iTBS + γtACS (t15 = 3.67, p-FDR = 0.0023; Figure 4A), but not for the iTBS + sham-tACS.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the control condition.

claim: No significant differences in PC-hippocampi connectivity were detected among the conditions before stimulation (all p > 0.05).
source: No significant differences were detected among the conditions before stimulation (all p > 0.05).
evidence: This confirms that baseline connectivity was similar across conditions.

claim: Stronger connectivity with the PC (MNI coordinates: x = 30, y = −70, z = 46; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1499; p = 0.000167) emerged when considering the right hippocampus as seed.
source: Moreover, stronger connectivity with the PC (MNI coordinates: x = 30, y = −70, z = 46; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1499; p = 0.000167) and with the posterior cingulate cortex emerged when considering the right hippocampus as seed (MNI coordinates: x = −14, y = −50, z = 12; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1295; p = 0.0001649) (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: This is supported by seed-to-voxel fMRI analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Stronger connectivity with the posterior cingulate cortex emerged when considering the right hippocampus as seed (MNI coordinates: x = −14, y = −50, z = 12; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1295; p = 0.0001649).
source: Moreover, stronger connectivity with the PC (MNI coordinates: x = 30, y = −70, z = 46; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1499; p = 0.000167) and with the posterior cingulate cortex emerged when considering the right hippocampus as seed (MNI coordinates: x = −14, y = −50, z = 12; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1295; p = 0.0001649) (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: This is supported by seed-to-voxel fMRI analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Similar results occurred considering the left hippocampus as seed, with an improved rs-FC with the PC (MNI coordinates: x = 30, y = −68, z = 44; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1525; p = 0.000163).
source: Finally, similar results occurred considering as seed the left hippocampus, with an improved rs-FC with the PC (MNI coordinates: x = 30, y = −68, z = 44; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1525; p = 0.000163) and with the posterior cingulate cortex (MNI coordinates: x = 20, y = −50, z = 12; |T15| > 3.20, k = 509; p = 0.022) (Figure 4B, left).
evidence: This is supported by seed-to-voxel fMRI analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Similar results occurred considering the left hippocampus as seed, with an improved rs-FC with the posterior cingulate cortex (MNI coordinates: x = 20, y = −50, z = 12; |T15| > 3.20, k = 509; p = 0.022).
source: Finally, similar results occurred considering as seed the left hippocampus, with an improved rs-FC with the PC (MNI coordinates: x = 30, y = −68, z = 44; |T15| > 3.20, k = 1525; p = 0.000163) and with the posterior cingulate cortex (MNI coordinates: x = 20, y = −50, z = 12; |T15| > 3.20, k = 509; p = 0.022) (Figure 4B, left).
evidence: This is supported by seed-to-voxel fMRI analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The white matter fibers connecting the PC with the temporal lobe form the bilateral Middle Longitudinal Fasciculus (MdLF).
source: We also reconstructed the white matter fibers connecting the PC with the temporal lobe in each subject, forming the bilateral Middle Longitudinal Fasciculus (MdLF), using Diffusion Tensor Images (DTI) tractography.
evidence: This is based on DTI tractography analysis.

claim: The structure of the MdLF measured through fractional anisotropy (FA) was related to the increased connectivity between PC and the hippocampi after dual iTBS + γtACS.
source: We found that the structure of the MdLF measured through fractional anisotropy (FA) was related to the increased connectivity between PC and the hippocampi after dual iTBS + γtACS.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between DTI and fMRI measures.
